t: Air Fryer Bacon: Times and Temperatures That Actually Work
d: Air fryer bacon times by thickness and doneness, with no-oil layouts, safe handling of hot grease, thick-cut and turkey bacon guidance.
x: Bacon is the food that convinces people to keep an air fryer on the counter: no splatter across the stovetop, and a strip that is crisp at the edges and still chewy in the middle if that is how you like it. It also produces more grease than almost anything else you will cook, and that grease is the whole story. Handle it correctly and bacon is simple. Two warnings before the chart First, times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer and your eyes, not the clock. Air fryer models differ in wattage, basket size and how close the element sits to the food, so a time that works in a 5.8-quart basket can burn bacon in a 2-quart one. Every time below is a range, and the last two minutes are yours to judge. Second, bacon is cured and smoked before it reaches your kitchen, so it is judged by appearance rather than by a target temperature. Turkey bacon is the exception: it is ground poultry, and ground poultry is cooked to 165°F / 74°C like any other ground meat. t: Air Fryer Chicken Time and Temperature Chart
d: Air fryer chicken time and temperature chart for breast, thighs, wings, tenders and drumsticks, with the 165°F / 74°C rule and frozen times.
x: Chicken is the food people most want to cook in an air fryer, and the food they most often get wrong. The window between juicy and sawdust is narrow, and it moves depending on how thick the piece is and whether it still has a bone. So this chart gives ranges you can start from. The number that decides whether dinner is safe is not on this page at all — it is the one your thermometer reads. Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. Wattage and basket size change the clock, but 165°F / 74°C does not change. Why time alone is unreliable for chicken A 6-ounce breast and an 8-ounce breast look almost identical in the basket. One finishes in 14 minutes and the other needs 20. Bone-in pieces cook slower near the bone. A crowded basket slows everything down because the air cannot circulate. An air fryer also browns the outside long before the inside is done. That is why a piece can look perfect, smell perfect and still be undercooked in the center. Color, juices and firmness are all guesses. A thermometer is a measurement. x: Air fryers cook fast because they move hot air hard. That same speed is why the first attempt at a new food usually goes wrong: a minute or two is the difference between crisp and dry. This is the chart I keep on the fridge. Use it as a starting point, then trust your own machine for the final minute. The one rule that matters more than any time on this chart Air fryer models differ hugely in wattage, basket size and how close the heating element sits to the food. t: Air Fryer Corn on the Cob: Times for Husked, In-Husk and Frozen
d: Air fryer corn on the cob times for husked, in-husk and frozen corn, with butter and oil handling and a note on reheating leftover corn safely.
x: Corn on the cob is the easiest side an air fryer makes. There is no pot of boiling water, no big kettle to drain, and the kernels come out with browned, slightly chewy spots that boiled corn never gets. It is also the one food on this site with no internal temperature to hit. Corn is a vegetable, and vegetables have no USDA safe internal temperature. Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer for meat and poultry. For corn, use the clock and your eyes, and remember that wattage and basket size change the time. There is no safe internal temperature for corn This matters because it is a common question. USDA publishes safe internal temperatures for meat, poultry, fish, eggs and reheated leftovers, not for vegetables. Corn has no target number, so anyone quoting one for the kernels is inventing it. What corn does have is a doneness you can see. The kernels turn bright yellow, some of them brown at the tips, and a kernel pressed with a fork gives slightly. If the kernels look pale and flat, they need more time. The exception is leftover corn. Once corn has been cooked and refrigerated, reheating it puts it under the standard for reheated food, which is 165°F / 74°C. t: Air Fryer Desserts Chart (Cookies, Cakes and More)
d: Air fryer desserts chart with times and temperatures for cookies, mug cakes, brownies, cinnamon rolls, donuts, baked apples, s'mores and churros.
x: Dessert is the hardest thing to cook in an air fryer, and it is not close. A savoury dish tells you when it is done with colour and a thermometer. A cookie tells you nothing until you bite it. The heating element sits inches from the food, the fan pushes dry air across the surface, and the basket is small. Cakes and cookies set on the outside while the middle is still batter. This is the category where a chart is a starting point and nothing more. Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. For desserts the thermometer measures the air, not the food: there is no safe internal temperature for a cookie. Use a toothpick. The rule that matters more than any number on this page There is no safe internal temperature for dessert. USDA internal-temperature guidance covers meat, poultry, eggs and leftovers, not cake batter, so anyone quoting you "the internal temperature of a brownie" is inventing a number. That leaves you two checks that actually work: Start checking early. If the chart says 15–18 min, look at 12 min. The last three minutes are where desserts go from underdone to ruined. Use the toothpick test. Insert a wooden toothpick or skewer into the centre and pull it out. A few moist crumbs are done. Wet batter is not. d: Air fryer hard boiled eggs by doneness, with soft, jammy and hard times, hot start and cold start methods, the ice bath and honest peeling notes.
x: Air frying eggs is not frying, and it is not boiling. You set whole eggs in the shell in the basket, run the machine low, and take them out with no pot to scrub. The results are real, and so are the limits. Here are the times by doneness, plus an honest answer on peeling. Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer for meat and a timer for eggs. Why people cook eggs in an air fryer Two reasons: hands-off cooking with no pot of water to heat, and the claim that air fryer eggs peel more easily, which this page deals with below. The trade is that a shell hides everything: you cannot see the yolk set, and you cannot read the center of an intact egg without breaking it. Time is your only control. d: Air fryer meal prep that actually holds up: what batches well, what turns to mush, the order to cook in, and the cooling and reheating rules.
x: An air fryer is a small, fast convection oven, which makes it a surprisingly good batch-cooking tool. It is also a small basket, so "batch" means several rounds, not one heroic load. The trick is planning the order. Cook in the wrong sequence and something sits raw on the counter while the machine is busy. Air fryer models differ in wattage, basket size and how close the element sits to the food. Treat every time below as a range, and verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Start with the two rules Rule one: pull food by temperature, not by the clock. Two air fryers of the same size can differ by several minutes on the same potato. Rule two: everything waiting its turn goes in the refrigerator. Not on the counter, not on the stovetop. Food that sits out while you cook the next batch is the main way meal prep goes wrong. What batches well, and what does not This is the table that saves the most time. Some foods reheat better than they cook the first time; others should never be prepped in advance. d: Air fryer meatball times for beef, pork, turkey and chicken, fresh or frozen, with the 160°F / 71°C ground meat rule and no medium-rare.
x: Meatballs are one of the best things an air fryer does: they brown on every side without a pan of oil, they hold their shape if you handle them once, and they freeze and reheat well. They are also the clearest example of a rule people get wrong: a meatball is ground meat, and ground meat has no medium-rare. Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. Wattage and basket size change the clock, but 160°F / 71°C and 165°F / 74°C do not change. The rule: ground meat has no medium-rare A whole steak can be served pink because the bacteria sit on the surface, where heat reaches them first. Grinding mixes that surface through the entire ball. Every part of the meatball is now surface, so the center has to reach the safe temperature. There is no pink middle that is safe by the same standard as a medium-rare steak. t: Air Fryer Pork Chops (Times by Thickness and Cut)
d: Air fryer pork chops by thickness, bone-in and boneless, with the 145°F / 63°C rule plus a 3 minute rest, brine times and breaded options.
x: Pork chops are lean, thin and easy to overcook — exactly the profile an air fryer handles badly if you guess. The target is lower than most people expect. Here is what matters: whole cuts of pork are done at 145°F / 63°C followed by a 3 minute rest, not 165°F / 74°C. Chops cooked to 165°F / 74°C are safe and gray, which is why a lot of people believe they do not like pork. Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. Wattage, basket size and the thickness of the chop change the clock, but 145°F / 63°C plus a 3 minute rest does not change. The 145°F / 63°C rule and the 3 minute rest USDA sets 145°F / 63°C for whole cuts of pork — chops, loin, tenderloin and roasts — with a 3 minute rest. The rest is part of the standard: the temperature has to hold for three minutes, and a chop pulled at 145°F / 63°C under foil does that. Ground pork is a different number: pork sausage and meatballs need 160°F / 71°C, because grinding moves surface bacteria through the whole mass. t: Air Fryer Potatoes (Times and Temperatures by Cut)
d: Air fryer potatoes by cut: wedges, cubes, baby potatoes, slices, hash browns and sweet potatoes, with temperatures, times and the soak-and-dry rule.
x: Potatoes are the highest-volume air fryer question there is. The difference between a crisp wedge and a pale, limp one is not the machine — it is starch, water and space in the basket. Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer for meat and your eyes for potatoes. Wattage, basket size and how full the basket is will move every number below. The starch rule: soak, then dry completely Cut potatoes release starch, and that starch is glue. It makes pieces stick together, steams the surfaces that touch, and leaves clumps that are crisp on one side and soft on the other. A 10–30 minute soak in cold water rinses that surface starch off. Drying matters more. Water on the surface has to evaporate before the potato can brown, so a wet potato steams first and crisps late. Drain, spread the pieces on a towel, and pat them dry. How much oil About 1 tablespoon of oil per pound of potatoes — roughly 15 mL per 450 g — and no more than 2 tablespoons for a full 2-pound basket. Toss until every piece has a faint sheen. More oil does not make crispier potatoes, just greasier ones, and the excess pools in the basket where it burns and smokes. Use a neutral oil with a high smoke point, and finish with butter or olive oil after the basket comes out. t: How to Reheat Leftovers in an Air Fryer (Chart and Times)
d: Reheat leftovers in an air fryer: pizza, fried chicken, fries, egg rolls and more, with times, temperatures and the 165°F / 74°C rule.
x: Reheating is the job an air fryer does better than anything else in the kitchen. Last night's pizza comes back with a crisp base instead of a chewy one, and fried chicken loses that damp coating. The reason is mechanical, not magical: hot moving air removes surface moisture and browns the outside, which is exactly what a microwave cannot do. Air fryer models differ in wattage, basket size and how close the element sits to the food. Treat every time below as a range, and verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Why the microwave disappoints and the air fryer does not A microwave heats food by agitating water molecules. The energy goes into the water inside the food, and the surface never gets hot and dry enough to brown. The differences follow from that: What happens Microwave Air fryer Heat source Water molecules absorb microwaves Hot air at 350–400°F / 177–205°C Surface Stays damp and soft Dries out and browns Steam Trapped inside the container Escapes through the basket Heating pattern Uneven, with hot and cold spots Even, from moving air Bread and pizza crust Chewy or leathery Crisp again in 3–5 min Breading and batter Turns limp Re-crisps rather than softening A covered microwave container traps the steam that a fried coating needs to lose. t: Air Fryer Shrimp: Times and Temperatures by Size and Type
d: Air fryer shrimp times by size for raw, frozen, shell-on, peeled and breaded shrimp, with why shrimp overcook in seconds and the 145°F / 63°C rule.
x: Shrimp is the fastest protein an air fryer cooks. It is also the least forgiving. A three-minute mistake turns sweet and springy into rubber, and no sauce fixes that. So the chart below is a starting point and the thermometer is the decision. Work out what you have — raw or cooked, peeled or in the shell, fresh or frozen — because that changes the time more than any temperature setting does. Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. Wattage and basket size change the clock, but 145°F / 63°C does not change. Why shrimp go from done to rubber in seconds A shrimp is thin. Most of it is less than half an inch from the surface, so heat reaches the center almost as fast as it reaches the outside. There is no thick core to buy you time, which is why the useful window is about 30 to 60 seconds. The second reason is water. Shrimp are roughly three-quarters water, and as they heat that water squeezes out and the muscle fibers tighten. Past the safe temperature they keep tightening, and the texture turns firm, then chalky, then rubbery. Shrimp also carry enzymes that turn them mushy if they sit at a lukewarm temperature too long. Shrimp are sold by count per pound, and the label is the size. U/15 means under 15 shrimp per pound, which is jumbo. 31/40 means 31 to 40 per pound, which is small. Buy by count, not by the word on the bag. The rule: 145°F / 63°C, USDA Seafood Safe inter

The rule: 145°F / 63°C, then rest 3 minutes USDA guidance for whole cuts of beef is 145°F / 63°C with a 3-minute rest. The rest is part of the standard, because the temperature holds and the juices redistribute while the meat sits. d: Air fryer tofu times and temperatures by cube size, plus pressing, firm versus extra-firm versus silken tofu, cornstarch coating and a crispiness fix.
x: Tofu is the one air fryer food where preparation decides everything. A wet, bare block comes out pale, soft, and stuck to the plate. The same block, pressed and dusted with cornstarch, comes out with a shell you can hear when you bite it. Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer for the numbers that matter, and treat every time below as a range. Wattage and basket size can move the clock by several minutes. Tofu is ready to eat, so there is no USDA minimum temperature This is the honest version. USDA publishes safe minimum internal temperatures for meat, poultry, fish and egg dishes. It does not publish one for tofu, because tofu is not a raw animal product and does not need to reach a safety temperature to be eaten. So there is no tofu temperature to hit, and this chart will not invent one. The temperatures below are cooking settings for browning and texture; the numbers that matter here are about storage and reheating. Tofu safety point Guidance Refrigerate cooked tofu within 2 hours Eat cooked tofu within 3–4 days Reheated tofu leftovers 165°F / 74°C A raw block from the fridge Ready to eat, no cooking needed Firm, extra-firm and silken: only two of these work Tofu is sold by water content, and water is the enemy of crispness. t: Air Fryer Turkey Breast: Times by Weight for Bone-In and Boneless
d: Air fryer turkey breast times by weight for bone-in, boneless, fresh and frozen, with brining, the 165°F / 74°C rule and why a whole turkey will not fit.
x: A turkey breast is the sensible answer to a holiday bird in an air fryer. It is small enough to fit, it cooks in about an hour, and it is almost all white meat, which is the part everyone reaches for first. A whole turkey is not an option in a normal air fryer, and that is a size fact rather than a technique problem. Below are the weights that do fit, the times they need, and the fix for a whole bird. Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. Wattage and basket size change the clock, but 165°F / 74°C does not change. The rule: 165°F / 74°C for all poultry Poultry Safe internal temperature Turkey breast, bone-in or boneless 165°F / 74°C Ground turkey and turkey sausage 165°F / 74°C Reheated turkey leftovers 165°F / 74°C USDA sets one number for poultry, and it does not change for white meat, dark meat, ground turkey or a reheated plate. There is no medium-rare turkey and no pink center that is safe by a lower standard. Probe the thickest part of the breast, away from the bone. Bone conducts heat differently and reads high, so a probe touching bone can tell you the turkey is done when the meat around it is not. If you are cooking a stuffed breast, the stuffing must also reach 165°F / 74°C. t: Air Fryer Vegetables Chart (Fresh and Frozen Times)
d: Printable air fryer vegetables chart for fresh and frozen vegetables, with the 1 tsp per cup oil rule, times, temperatures and crispiness fixes.
x: Vegetables are where an air fryer surprises people. The same machine that rescues frozen fries turns broccoli into something with browned edges and a little chew, in under 10 minutes and without heating the kitchen. They are also where people give up fastest, because a dry vegetable in hot moving air does not roast. It dehydrates, then scorches at the tips. Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer for meat, and your eyes and a fork for vegetables. The oil rule: about 1 teaspoon per cup This is the single change that fixes most disappointing air fryer vegetables. Use roughly 1 tsp of oil per cup of cut vegetables — about 1 tbsp for a 4-cup basket — and toss until every piece has a faint sheen. No pools in the bottom of the bowl, no dry patches. Oil does two jobs here. It carries heat across the surface so the vegetable browns instead of drying, and it holds any seasoning you add. Vegetables with a dry surface burn at the thin edges while the middle stays raw. Two more rules matter as much as the oil: Cut evenly. A 1-inch piece and a 2-inch piece of the same carrot cannot finish together. Stay in one layer. Two layers of vegetables steam. Steamed vegetables are soft and pale, and more time will not fix that. t: How to Clean an Air Fryer (Schedule and Safe Methods)
d: How to clean an air fryer: a daily, weekly and monthly schedule, dishwasher-safe parts, baked-on grease fixes, element care and odour removal.
x: Most air fryers die early for one of two reasons: the basket coating gives up, or grease bakes onto the element and starts to smoke. Both are preventable, and both are cleaning problems. An air fryer is easy to clean if you do it often. The two mistakes people make — soaking the whole appliance and scrubbing with abrasive pads — are exactly the ones that cause damage. Cleaning guidance varies by appliance model — read your manual before you soak, scrub or dishwasher anything. Wattage and basket size have nothing to do with cleaning, but the finish on your basket decides everything. Daily, weekly and monthly Daily is the basket and the drawer. Weekly is the element, the guard and the outer shell. Monthly is the deep clean and an inspection. Do the daily job while the unit is still slightly warm, not hot and not cold, because warm grease wipes away and cold grease has to be chipped. When What How After every use Basket and crisper plate Warm water, dish soap, soft sponge, dry fully After every use Drawer cavity Wipe with a damp cloth once cool Weekly Heating element and guard Unplug and cool, dry soft brush, damp cloth Weekly Exterior shell and handle Damp cloth, then dry, never wet the vents Monthly Baked-on grease on the basket Baking soda paste or vinegar steam Monthly Rubber seals and element guard Inspect for cracking, clean around them Monthly Cord and plug Look for fraying

t: Oven to Air Fryer Conversion Chart (Temperatures and Times)
d: Convert any oven recipe to an air fryer: lower the temperature about 25°F / 15°C, cut the time about 20 percent, and know when conversion fails.
x: An air fryer is a small convection oven with the element inches from the food. That proximity is why an oven recipe overcooks in it: same food, same temperature, much more heat where it counts. The fix is three adjustments. They are rules of thumb, not a formula. Air fryer models differ in wattage, basket size and how close the element sits to the food. Treat every time below as a range, and verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. The three general rules Rule one: lower the temperature by roughly 25°F / 15°C. Air fryer dials are usually calibrated at the element, not at the food, and the food sits much closer to it. Rule two: cut the time by roughly 20 percent. A 25–30 min oven step becomes about 20–24 min. Rule three: check early. Open the basket at about two-thirds of the converted time. Once something is over-browned, there is no way back. Two constraints matter as much as the numbers. The basket holds one layer, so a sheet-pan recipe becomes two or three rounds. And most air fryers need a 3–5 min preheat for browning. Oven to air fryer conversion chart Find your oven temperature, then set the air fryer to the middle column and start at the low end of the time.
